title: Seeing 1, 2 or 3 at a glance
keyIdea: You can see one, two or three things fast, without counting. A quick look is enough. Moving things apart does not change how many. Big or tiny, each thing is one.

kid: Look fast! One dot. Two dots. Three dots. You can see how many. You do not need to count.
Three dots can sit in a line. They can make a hat shape. Each time it is three.
Push the dots far apart. Still three! Push them close. Still three!
A big ball is one. A tiny bead is one. Two big balls are less than three tiny beads.
adult: Seeing a small amount at a glance, without counting, is called subitising. Perceptual subitising works for up to about three or four items, and it is one of the first parts of number sense. The EYFS Early Learning Goal for Number asks children to subitise (recognise quantities without counting) up to 5; at three and four, aim for 1, 2 and 3.

Subitising links a quantity to its number name, which builds cardinality: the idea that a number tells how many are in a whole group. Dice patterns, fingers and small groups of toys all help. Change the arrangement often (in a line, a triangle, a slant) so your child learns the amount and not just one picture.

Common mistakes to watch for: thinking that spreading a group out makes more (the number stays the same; this is called conservation of number), judging by size so that two big things seem more than three small ones, and guessing a number at random instead of looking. Counting one by one is fine as a check, but praise the quick look.

In the lab your child sees dots flash on a plate and says how many, drags three dots far apart to find it is still three, matches dice faces to birds on a fence, shows small groups of apples with fingers, and sorts big and tiny things by how many.

familyTip: At snack time, put out 1, 2 or 3 raisins, cover them with your hand, then lift it for a second. Ask how many. Swap the pattern each time, and let your child do it to you too.

visual.caption: How many at a glance? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: quick looks at dots, spread dots apart, match dice to birds, show groups with fingers, and sort big and tiny things by how many.

practice.prompt: You see 3 dots in a line. Then they make a triangle. How many now?
practice.hint: Did any dot come or go, or did they just move?
practice.explain: Still 3. The dots only moved into a new shape, so the number stays the same.

practice.prompt: Mia has {n} cars. She sees 2 big trucks and 3 tiny cars on a mat. Which group has more?
practice.hint: Look at how many, not how big each one is.
practice.explain: 3 tiny cars is more than 2 big trucks. Size does not change how many. Mia's own {n} cars are a different group.

practice.prompt: A dice shows 2 dots. Which group matches it?
practice.hint: The dice has 2 dots. Find the group with the same number.
practice.explain: 2 birds match 2 dots. They look different, but both are two.

practice.prompt: Leo is {n}. He sees 1 apple. How many fingers show the apple?
practice.hint: Show the same number of fingers as there are apples.
practice.explain: 1 apple, so 1 finger. Leo's age, {n}, is not about the apples.

pool.prompt: Dots flash for a moment: one at the top, two at the bottom. How many?
pool.hint: One and two make a little triangle. Picture it.
pool.explain: 3. One dot on top and two below make a triangle of three.

pool.prompt: The plate is empty. How many dots are on it?
pool.hint: Look closely. Is there anything on the plate at all?
pool.explain: None, also called zero. An empty plate has no dots.

pool.prompt: {n} children watch 2 buttons roll far apart. How many buttons now?
pool.hint: Did a button come or go, or did they only roll?
pool.explain: Still 2 buttons. Rolling apart does not add or take away a button, however many children watch.

pool.prompt: 1 big elephant or 3 tiny ants. Which group has more?
pool.hint: Each animal is one, big or tiny. Look at how many.
pool.explain: 3 ants is more than 1 elephant. A big thing is still just one.

pool.prompt: Sam is {n}. He sees 3 birds and says three fast, without counting. What did he do?
choices: He saw it at a glance
pool.hint: Fast, without counting one by one, is called what?
pool.explain: He saw 3 at a glance. Seeing a small group fast is called subitising. Sam's age, {n}, does not matter here.

pool.hint: Look for the face with the most dots: one, two, three.
pool.explain: Three dots on a slant is 3. One dot is 1, and two corner dots are 2.

pool.prompt: Show 2 with your fingers. How many go up?
pool.hint: Put up one finger for each thing, until you have two.
pool.explain: 2 fingers up show 2. All your fingers would be 5.

pool.prompt: 3 socks in a row, or 3 socks in a pile. Which has more?
pool.hint: Count each group once to check. Is one group bigger?
pool.explain: They are the same. Both are 3 socks. A row or a pile does not change how many.
